newsitem.title: INDONESIA: FEATURE-Indonesia's capital strives to preserve heritage.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Indonesia's capital strives to preserve heritage.

text.p: As late as the 1930s Batavia, as Indonesia's capital Jakarta was then called, was a favorite destination of Europeans living in Singapore for its picturesque Dutch colonial houses and tree-lined streets.
Sixty years later, guidebooks describe Jakarta as Asia's least visited capital.
Much of Jakarta's past grandeur has disappeared as the city of 10 million people mutated into one of Asia's booming metropolises, with all the attendant squalor, pollution and poverty.
It has this vast country's most modern buildings -- but also its dirtiest slums and a reputation as run-down, poorly planned and home to some of the worst traffic jams in Asia.
But efforts are being made to reverse this trend, starting with a programme to preserve its fading colonial buildings and palaces.
POOR RECORD OF CONSERVATION

Located on an alluvial lowland on the north coast of Java island, Jakarta currently has 113 protected buildings, most of them built during the 350 years of Dutch colonial occupation which officially ended in 1949.
The lucky ones such as the 18th century, double-storeyed Presidential Palace, are too important to be destroyed.

But others face the threat of demolition as they sit on prime real estate in business districts. Some are falling into decay as their owners complain of a lack of funds and incentives to maintain them.

Adolf Heuken, a German-born priest and writer of a book called "Historical Sights of Jakarta", said the problem facing the city was the lack of awareness of the value of old buildings, which he said give a city its character.

"I think the problem is ignorance. Eighty percent of Jakartans come from the rest of the archipelago and there have not been efforts to let them know about Jakarta's history," he told Reuters in an interview.
"When it comes to conserving historical buildings, Jakarta has a very poor record," he said.

Last year, a protected house in west Jakarta which featured the so-called "old Indie style" of a projecting roof and wide verandahs, was taken off the list of protected buildings for unclear reasons and demolished.
A COLOURFUL, COSMOPOLITAN BACKGROUND
Jakarta once earned the nickname the "Queen of the East" because of its architectural splendour.

It was founded in 1527 after a combined force of Moslem troops from the Sultanate of Demak in eastern Java and from nearby Banten conquered the port of Sunda Kelapa and called it "Jayakarta". The city had become the centre of a network of sea-based trading posts between Cape Town in South Africa and Nagasaki in Japan.
It was also a meeting point of people of all races and religions. Heuken writes in his book:

"French Calvinist services were held in the City Hall, Moslem Indians prayed at their mosques, Chinese worshipped in Hakka. Arabs followed their Sayid leader and German Lutherans sang their hymns in a church downtown."
In May 1619, the Dutch came to the archipelago in search of spices. They destroyed Jayakarta and established Batavia, which started centuries of colonisation.
The name Jakarta was used after the Japanese occupied Indonesia in 1942.
During the colonial period, the city had hundreds of Dutch-style mansions and country houses featuring porticos and wide verandahs, the ideal design for the tropical climate.
Palaces in a classic style inspired by the Greeks and Romans were also common features, while the art deco style boomed in the first quarter of the century.
Other treasures included Chinese temples dating back to the 16th century, old mosques and Moorish houses built by the descendants of Arab traders.
NEW EFFORTS TO PRESERVE HERITAGE
Jakarta has embarked on an ambitious plan to revive the old city, which covers an area of 139 hectares near the Sunda Kelapa harbour, as a tourist attraction.

"We understand that our perception of conservation is not unified yet. That's why we are trying now to improve awareness," said Haswidi Taufik, chief of the city's History, Museum and Conservation office.

"We are thinking about giving incentives to owners of old houses by, for example, giving a discount on taxes. We are thinking of shifting the function of old buildings into hotels or cafes in order to boost their economic value," he said.
At least seven old buildings are to be converted into a hotel, but the government admitted it was tough to attract investors to invest in an area known for its chronic traffic jams and slums.
The old part of the city boasts warehouses built between 1663 and 1669, a lookout tower and a 18th century former city hall whose architecture resembled the Royal Palace in Amsterdam.

Heuken said the government had to show more commitment to protecting the city's heritage. "A city should have a character. Now everything seems to be similar concrete blocks. Because buildings are similar everywhere, people do not care about the city," he said.
Taufik said he was optimistic the project would bear fruit.
"We have seen the political will from the City Council and the governor in preserving our heritage and I don't see any problems in funding either."
Heuken said he believed renovation was not enough, adding that renovated buildings could be used for other purposes.

"We can turn the 300-year-old warehouses into schools, for instance. Warehouses need to be protected because they are witnesses of the history that Christopher Columbus discovered America on his way to search for spices here," he said.
